name: Lava Lamp
brief: Build a fragment shader that looks like a lava lamp: three layers of noise at different scales (coarse ~2, medium ~5, fine ~10), blended together and tinted with a blue-to-orange gradient, with a glow effect on top.

scoring.description: Tests complex topology — can the AI wire a multi-node graph correctly?

name: Slow Lava
brief: Build a fragment shader that looks like slow-moving lava. Use noise with deep red, orange, and black colors. The movement should feel organic and slow. Tune parameters to make it look right — the colors need to be hot (reds/oranges), and the noise movement should be subtle.

scoring.description: Tests parameter hunting — can the AI find the right values within constrained ranges?

name: Kaleidoscope Refactor
brief: Start with a simple gradient shader (Gradient → Output). Refactor it to add 4-way kaleidoscope symmetry: mirror the gradient in both X and Y axes so the output has a symmetrical pattern with 4 mirrored quadrants. The final shader should show the gradient repeated as a kaleidoscope.

scoring.description: Tests structural reasoning — can the AI rewire a graph by inserting new nodes?

name: Vignette Addition
brief:
Here is a working noise shader:

Noise(scale=3, seed=1) → Output

Add a dark vignette effect that darkens the edges of the output without changing the noise pattern in the center. The vignette should be subtle — the center should be unchanged, and the corners should be about 50% darker. Do not break the existing noise output.

scoring.description: Tests surgical precision — can the AI make targeted changes without collateral damage?

name: Dreamy Blur
brief: Create a soft, dreamy shader. Start with a procedural texture source, then apply a strong blur (radius 8 or higher). The output should look hazy and out-of-focus, like looking through frosted glass.

scoring.description: Tests the Blur primitive specifically — can the AI wire it with appropriate parameters?

name: DVD Interlace
brief: Create a fragment shader that applies DVD-style MPEG frame interlacing artefacts to a texture input. The output should show a combing effect where alternating horizontal rows are offset by half a pixel. Use gl_FragCoord.y to determine the row — even rows should be shifted half a pixel to the right, odd rows should not be shifted. The effect should look like classic interlaced video: a characteristic sawtooth/comb edge pattern on diagonal lines.

scoring.description: Tests per-pixel coordinate logic — can the AI compose mod/floor/offset effects from available primitives?

name: Rutt-Etra Scanline Displacement
brief: Create a fragment shader applying the classic Rutt-Etra video effect. Sample a texture, then for each pixel: (1) compute luminance from the texture color using standard Rec.709 coefficients (0.299R + 0.587G + 0.114B), (2) compute which horizontal scanline the pixel belongs to using FragCoord/Floor/Mod, (3) displace the Y-coordinate by an amount proportional to the luminance, (4) resample the texture at the displaced coordinates, (5) overlay a scanline pattern so individual lines are visible. Use Texture, FragCoord, Swizzle, Multiply, Add, Floor, Mod, and Displace primitives. Tune Displace amount (0.02-0.1) and scanline count (200-300).

scoring.description: Tests luminance extraction from primitives, coordinate math for scanlines, and UV displacement composition.

name: Geodesic Sphere
brief: Create a geodesic sphere by subdividing an icosahedron. Generate vertex data for subdivision levels 0 through 4 (level 0 = 20 faces, level 4 = 5120 faces). Each subdivision splits every triangle into 4 by creating midpoints on each edge and projecting them onto the unit sphere. Render the result with vertex shader rotation and fragment shader lighting (red on black), cycling through levels 0-4 over 60 seconds.

scoring.description: Tests algorithmic geometry generation — can the AI implement icosahedron subdivision with correct vertex projection and face reconstruction?
